text: Royal Eason Ingersoll (20 June 1883 – 20 May 1976) was a United States Navy four-star admiral who served as Commander in Chief, U.S. Atlantic Fleet (CINCLANT) from January 1, 1942 to late 1944; Commander, Western Sea Frontier from late 1944 to 1946; and Deputy Commander in Chief, U.S. Fleet/Deputy Chief of Naval Operations (DCOMINCH/DCNO) from late 1944 to late 1945. Born in Washington, D.C., on 20 June 1883, he was second in a line of three generations of U.S. Naval officers: his father, Rear Admiral Royal R. Ingersoll—United States Naval Academy class of 1868—and his son, Lieutenant Royal Rodney Ingersoll II—USNA class of 1934—was killed in a friendly fire accident on board the aircraft carrier Hornet (CV-8) on 4 June 1942 during the naval Battle of Midway. Ingersoll graduated from the Naval Academy in 1905, along with Chester W. Nimitz, and reported as a passed midshipman to the battleship Missouri (BB-11). In August 1905, he was assigned special temporary duty to attend the Russian-Japanese Peace Conference at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery, Maine. After being detached from the Missouri in May 1906, he served briefly on the Marietta (PG-15) and later the Hancock (AP-3), then assisted in fitting out the Connecticut (BB-18) at the New York Navy Yard, serving on that battleship from her commissioning on 29 September 1906 until October 1907. He served as an instructor of Seamanship and International Law, and later of English, at the Naval Academy between 1911 and 1913, preceding his assignment to the Asiatic Squadron, where he joined the armored cruiser Saratoga (ACR-2), the flagship of the U.S. Asiatic Fleet, serving briefly as her First Lieutenant and later as Aide and Flag Lieutenant to the Chief-of-Staff of the Asiatic Fleet's Commander. He returned to the United States and on 1 June 1916 reported as Assistant for Communications and Communication Officer in the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations, Navy Department. He wrote that the work in this office intensified as diplomatic tensions with Germany rose, and on 2 February 1917, when diplomatic relations with Germany were broken, the workload overwhelmed the office. For organizing the greatly expanded Naval Communications Office during World War I, he was awarded the Navy Cross and cited "for distinguished service in the line of his profession in organizing, developing, and administering the Communication Office of the Navy Department." After the Armistice in November 1918, he was ordered to join Admiral William S. Benson, USN, then Chief of Naval Operations, to establish a communication office for that commission. In February 1919, he returned home aboard the George Washington with the Presidential party, handling messages for President Woodrow Wilson across the Atlantic. In March 1919, he rejoined the Connecticut as her executive officer until September 1920, then transferred to the Arizona (BB-39). In June 1921, he reported to the Navy Department for a tour of duty in the Office of Naval Intelligence, and on 26 March 1924, assumed command of the Nokomis (SP-609). Under his command, the gunboat was fitted out as a survey ship and cruised in the Cuban–Haitian area, producing new charts of the north coast of Cuba. Completing the Senior Course at the Naval War College in Newport, Rhode Island in June 1927, he served as a member of that staff the following year. In June 1928, he reported as Assistant Chief of Staff to Commander Battle Fleet in the California (BB-44) and continued in similar duty on the Staff when Admiral William V. Pratt became Commander in Chief, United States Fleet, with his flag in the Texas (BB-35). In August 1930, he was assigned to the Division of Fleet Training, Office of the Chief of Naval Operations, Navy Department, where he served until May 1933. He then became Commanding Officer of the heavy cruiser Augusta (CA-31), and in November 1933, was transferred to the Mare Island Naval Shipyard to fit out the San Francisco (CA-38), which he commanded from her commissioning on 10 February 1934 until June 1935. His three-year assignment in the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations as Director of the War Plans Division included his role in June 1936 as Technical Assistant to the American Delegation at the London Naval Conference (1935–36). He again traveled to London in December 1937, addressing requirements arising from the London Naval Treaty limiting naval armament. On 16 July 1938, Ingersoll took command of Cruiser Division Six of the Scouting Force, with his flag in the cruiser Minneapolis (CA-36). Two years later, he returned to the Office of the Chief of Naval Operations as assistant to the Chief, and on 1 January 1942, with the rank of Vice Admiral, was designated Commander in Chief, U.S. Atlantic Fleet, with the Augusta as his flagship. Ingersoll was promoted to the rank of admiral on 1 July 1942 and broke his flag on the converted yacht USS Vixen (PG-53) on 17 July. Having organized the movements of thousands of ships across the Atlantic to deliver men and supplies at the precise hour for the North African landings in November 1942, he also planned the composition of naval escort forces to ensure the safe arrival of troop convoys. Following the North African invasion, the Atlantic Fleet was tasked with running troop convoys and transporting stores, munitions, and fuel to the United Kingdom and the Mediterranean, as well as operating convoys along the coast of Brazil and continuously conducting the anti-submarine war, a primary concern since the outbreak of hostilities. Ingersoll is generally credited with solving the U-boat and Atlantic logistics problems. Additionally, he was responsible for the defense of the Western Hemisphere by U.S. naval forces and made changes in the disposition of air and surface forces stationed in North and South America. For his service in this command, he was awarded the Distinguished Service Medal and cited as a "forceful and resolute leader under the critical conditions existing throughout a period of approximately three years... against a determined and ruthless enemy intent on world domination..." In November 1944, he was detached from the Atlantic Fleet and became Commander Western Sea Frontier, with headquarters in San Francisco. In addition to commanding naval forces protecting shipping in coastal waters, he managed the flow of supplies to the Pacific Fleet through West Coast ports. In this role, he held the status of Deputy Commander in Chief, U.S. Fleet, and Deputy Chief of Naval Operations. After the navy's reorganization in October 1945, he continued as Commander Western Sea Frontier until 10 April 1946, when he was relieved of all active duty pending his retirement, which became official on 1 August 1946. Ingersoll was married in 1910 to Louise Van Harlingen of Atlanta, Georgia, and had two children. He died on 20 May 1976. In 1979, Mrs. Louise Ingersoll was the sponsor for USS Ingersoll (DD-990); their daughter, Alice Jean Ingersoll Nagle, acted as proxy sponsor. Their son, Royal Rodney II, had been (with Admiral Ingersoll's father) the namesake of the USS Ingersoll (DD-652). In addition to the Navy Cross and the Distinguished Service Medal, Ingersoll was awarded the World War I Victory Medal; the American Defense Service Medal; European-African-Middle Eastern Campaign Medal; and the World War II Victory Medal. He also received the Chevalier of the Legion of Honor from the French Government, the Order of Naval Merit (Grand Cross) from the Government of Brazil, and the Grand Officer of the Order of Orange Nassau with Swords from the Government of The Netherlands.
